title: UNIT 4: STATIC AND CURRENT ELECTRICITY
notes:
✓ Electricity → Physical phenomenon associated with the presence and flow of electric charge.

◆ STATIC ELECTRICITY
✓ Static electricity → Accumulation of electric charge on an object.

◆ CURRENT ELECTRICITY
✓ Current electricity → Continuous flow of electric charge through a conducting path.

title: 4.1 CHARGES IN NATURE
notes:
✓ Electric charge → Exists in two types: positive and negative.

◆ TYPES OF ELECTRIC CHARGE
✓ Positive charge → Associated with protons.
✓ Negative charge → Associated with electrons.

◆ NEUTRAL BODY
✓ Neutral body → Contains equal amounts of positive and negative charge, giving zero net charge.

✓ Body gains electrons → Becomes negatively charged.
✓ Body loses electrons → Becomes positively charged.

◆ UNIT OF CHARGE
✓ SI unit → Coulomb (C).

✓ Elementary charge:
e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C

✓ Electron charge → −e.
✓ Proton charge → +e.

◆ QUANTIZATION OF CHARGE
✓ Electric charge → Occurs in discrete amounts:
q = ne

✓ n → Integer.
✓ e → 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

◆ CONSERVATION OF CHARGE
✓ Electric charge → Cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be transferred from one body to another.

◆ KEY IDEA
✓ Like charges → Repel: (+,+) or (−,−).
✓ Unlike charges → Attract: (+,−).

title: 4.2 METHODS OF CHARGING A BODY
notes:
✓ Charging → Process of electrifying a body by adding or removing electrons.

◆ MAIN METHODS
✓ Charging by rubbing.
✓ Charging by conduction.
✓ Charging by induction.

◆ CHARGING BY RUBBING
✓ Rubbing two different materials → Causes electrons to transfer from one material to the other.

✓ Object gains electrons → Negative.
✓ Object loses electrons → Positive.
✓ Two objects → Acquire opposite charges.

✓ Example → Rubbing a comb with hair.

◆ CHARGING BY CONDUCTION
✓ Conduction → A charged body is brought into direct contact with a neutral conductor.

✓ Electrons → Move between the bodies until charge is redistributed.

✓ Neutral body → Acquires the same type of charge as the charging body, but generally with a weaker charge.

◆ CHARGING BY INDUCTION
✓ Induction → A charged object is brought near a neutral conductor without touching it, causing charges inside the conductor to redistribute.

✓ Conductor grounded while charged object is nearby → Electrons can enter or leave.

✓ Ground removed first, then charging object removed → Conductor is left with a net charge opposite to the inducing charge.

◆ GROUNDING
✓ Grounding → Connecting a conductor to Earth so electrons can flow to or from the conductor.

✓ Earth → Acts as a huge charge reservoir.

◆ KEY IDEA
✓ Rubbing → Friction/contact between materials.
✓ Conduction → Direct contact.
✓ Induction → Charging without direct contact.

title: 4.3 THE ELECTROSCOPE
notes:
✓ Electroscope → Sensitive device used to detect electric charge on a body.

◆ GOLD-LEAF ELECTROSCOPE
✓ Main parts → Metal plate/knob • conducting metal rod • two thin gold leaves • insulating support • glass container.

◆ WORKING PRINCIPLE
✓ Charged object approaches metal plate → Charges inside the electroscope redistribute by induction.

✓ Two leaves → Acquire like charges and repel each other, causing them to diverge.

◆ USES
✓ Detect whether an object is charged.
✓ Detect the type of charge when compared with a known charge.
✓ Demonstrate electrostatic induction.
✓ Demonstrate conduction and charge redistribution.

◆ IMPORTANT
✓ Leaf divergence → Indicates presence of charge.
✓ Charged object removed → Induced charge redistribution disappears and the leaves can collapse.

title: 4.4 ELECTRICAL DISCHARGE
notes:
✓ Electrical discharge → Rapid transfer of electric charge from a charged body through a conducting path.

✓ Charged body → Can be discharged by connecting it to a conductor or to Earth.

◆ SPARK
✓ Spark → Visible example of electrical discharge through air.

◆ LIGHTNING
✓ Lightning → Huge electrical discharge associated with thunderstorms.

✓ Charges separate within a cloud → A large potential difference develops between regions of the cloud or between cloud and ground.

✓ Strong electric field → Ionizes the air and creates a conducting path.

✓ Large amount of charge → Rapidly moves through the path, producing a lightning flash.

✓ Rapid heating and expansion of air → Produce thunder.

◆ GROUNDING
✓ Grounding → Provides a safe path for excess charge to flow into the Earth.

◆ LIGHTNING SAFETY
✓ During thunderstorms → Avoid exposed high places, isolated trees and conductive objects.
✓ Lightning conductors → Provide safer paths for discharge.

✓ KEY IDEA → Discharge removes excess charge by providing a path for charge to move.

title: 4.5 COULOMB'S LAW OF ELECTROSTATICS
notes:
✓ Coulomb's law → Gives the electrostatic force between two point charges.

F = k|q₁q₂|/r²

✓ q₁, q₂ → Charges.
✓ r → Separation between their centers.
✓ k → Coulomb constant.

✓ In vacuum/air approximately:
k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²

◆ FORCE DEPENDENCE
✓ F ∝ |q₁q₂|
✓ F ∝ 1/r²

✓ Increasing either charge → Increases the force.
✓ Increasing separation → Decreases the force according to the inverse-square law.

✓ Like charges → Repulsive force.
✓ Unlike charges → Attractive force.

◆ DIRECTION
✓ Electrostatic force → Acts along the straight line joining the two charges.

✓ KEY IDEA → Coulomb's law is the electrostatic analogue of the inverse-square form of gravitational interaction, but electric forces can be attractive or repulsive.

title: 4.6 THE ELECTRIC FIELD
notes:
✓ Electric field → Region around a charge where another electric charge experiences an electric force.

◆ TEST CHARGE
✓ Test charge → Small positive charge used to test the existence and strength of an electric field.

✓ Test charge → Is assumed small enough not to significantly disturb the existing field.

◆ ELECTRIC FIELD STRENGTH
E = F/q

✓ Therefore:
F = Eq

✓ SI unit → N/C.
✓ Electric field → Is a vector quantity.

◆ FIELD DIRECTION
✓ Direction of E → Direction of the force on a positive test charge.
✓ Negative charge → Experiences electric force opposite to the field direction.

◆ FIELD OF A POINT CHARGE
E = k|Q|/r²

✓ Q → Source charge.
✓ r → Distance from the source charge.

◆ FIELD-LINE PROPERTIES
✓ Field lines → Originate from positive charges.
✓ Field lines → Terminate on negative charges or extend to infinity.
✓ Field lines → Never cross one another.
✓ Field lines → Are perpendicular to the surface of a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium.
✓ Greater line density → Represents a stronger electric field.
✓ Field lines → Point away from positive charges and toward negative charges.

✓ KEY IDEA → Electric field describes the force effect of a charge on the surrounding space.

title: 4.7 ELECTRIC CIRCUITS
notes:
✓ Electric circuit → Complete path through which electric charges can flow.

◆ MAIN COMPONENTS
✓ Cell/battery → Source of electrical energy and potential difference.
✓ Connecting wires → Conducting path.
✓ Switch → Opens or closes the circuit.
✓ Load → Device that converts electrical energy into other forms, such as a lamp or motor.
✓ Resistor → Opposes current.
✓ Ammeter → Measures current.
✓ Voltmeter → Measures potential difference.

◆ CLOSED CIRCUIT
✓ Complete conducting path → Charges can flow → Current exists.

◆ OPEN CIRCUIT
✓ Broken/incomplete path → Current is zero → Load does not operate.

◆ CIRCUIT DIAGRAM
✓ Electrical components → Are represented using standard symbols rather than drawings of their physical appearance.

✓ KEY IDEA → A source provides potential difference, while the closed conducting path allows current to flow through the load.

title: 4.8 CURRENT, VOLTAGE AND OHM'S LAW
notes:
◆ ELECTRIC CURRENT
✓ Electric current → Rate of flow of electric charge.

I = ΔQ/Δt

✓ For steady current:
I = Q/t

✓ SI unit → Ampere (A).
✓ 1 A = 1 C/s.

◆ POTENTIAL DIFFERENCE / VOLTAGE
✓ Potential difference → Work done per unit charge in moving charge between two points.

V = W/Q

✓ Therefore:
W = VQ

✓ SI unit → Volt (V).
✓ 1 V = 1 J/C.

◆ RESISTANCE
✓ Resistance → Opposition a conductor offers to the flow of electric charge.

R = V/I

✓ SI unit → Ohm (Ω).
✓ 1 Ω = 1 V/A.

◆ OHM'S LAW
✓ For a conductor at constant temperature → V ∝ I.

V = IR

✓ Therefore:
I = V/R
R = V/I

◆ OHMIC MATERIAL
✓ Ohmic material → Material that obeys Ohm's law over a given range and has approximately constant resistance at constant temperature.

◆ FACTORS AFFECTING RESISTANCE
R = ρL/A

✓ Resistance → Increases with length L.
✓ Resistance → Decreases with cross-sectional area A.
✓ Resistance → Depends on the material through resistivity ρ.

◆ TEMPERATURE
✓ Metallic conductor resistance → Generally increases as temperature increases.

title: 4.8 RESISTIVITY AND CONDUCTIVITY
notes:
◆ RESISTIVITY
✓ Resistivity → Material property that indicates how strongly a material opposes electric current.

ρ = RA/L

✓ Therefore:
R = ρL/A

✓ SI unit → Ω·m.

✓ High resistivity → Material strongly opposes current.
✓ Low resistivity → Material allows current to flow more easily.

◆ CONDUCTIVITY
✓ Conductivity → Reciprocal of resistivity.

σ = 1/ρ

✓ High conductivity → Low resistivity.
✓ Low conductivity → High resistivity.

✓ KEY IDEA → Resistance depends on the dimensions and material of a conductor, while resistivity is primarily a property of the material.

title: 4.9 COMBINATION OF RESISTORS IN A CIRCUIT
notes:
✓ Resistors → Can be connected mainly in series or parallel.

◆ SERIES CONNECTION
✓ Series connection → Resistors are connected one after another in a single path.

✓ Equivalent resistance:
Req = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + ... + Rₙ

◆ SERIES RULES
✓ Same current → Flows through every resistor.
✓ Total voltage → Is divided among the resistors.
✓ Equivalent resistance → Is greater than any individual resistance.

V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃ + ...

◆ PARALLEL CONNECTION
✓ Parallel connection → Resistors are connected across the same two points, creating multiple current paths.

✓ Equivalent resistance:
1/Req = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃ + ... + 1/Rₙ

◆ PARALLEL RULES
✓ Same voltage → Exists across each branch.
✓ Total current → Is the sum of branch currents.
✓ Equivalent resistance → Is less than the smallest individual resistance.

I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃ + ...

✓ KEY IDEA → SERIES → Same current.
✓ PARALLEL → Same voltage.

title: 4.9 SERIES & PARALLEL CIRCUITS
notes:
◆ SERIES
Req = R₁ + R₂ + ...

✓ I = I₁ = I₂ = I₃
✓ V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃

✓ One component disconnected → The whole path is broken.

◆ PARALLEL
1/Req = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ...

✓ V = V₁ = V₂ = V₃
✓ I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃

✓ One branch disconnected → Current can still flow through the other branches.

◆ HOUSEHOLD CIRCUITS
✓ Electrical appliances → Are generally connected in parallel so that each appliance receives the supply voltage and can operate independently.

title: 4.10 VOLTMETER AND AMMETER CONNECTION IN A CIRCUIT
notes:
◆ AMMETER
✓ Ammeter → Measures electric current.
✓ Ammeter → Is connected in series with the component whose current is being measured.
✓ Ideal ammeter → Has very small resistance.

◆ VOLTMETER
✓ Voltmeter → Measures potential difference between two points.
✓ Voltmeter → Is connected in parallel across the component.
✓ Ideal voltmeter → Has very large resistance.

◆ WHY?
✓ Ammeter in series → Allows the circuit current to pass through the meter.
✓ Voltmeter in parallel → Measures the potential difference between two points while drawing very little current.

◆ IMPORTANT
✓ Ammeter directly across a voltage source → Can cause a very large current and may damage the meter or circuit.

title: 4.11 ELECTRICAL SAFETY IN GENERAL AND LOCAL CONTEXT
notes:
✓ Electricity → Is useful but can cause electric shock, burns, fires and damage to equipment when handled incorrectly.

◆ SAFETY RULES
✓ Never touch electrical equipment with wet hands.
✓ Avoid damaged or exposed wires.
✓ Do not overload sockets or extension cords.
✓ Use properly rated fuses and circuit breakers.
✓ Disconnect power before repairing electrical equipment.
✓ Use proper insulation.
✓ Keep electrical devices away from water.
✓ Never insert objects into electrical outlets.
✓ Use proper grounding/earthing.
✓ Keep children away from dangerous electrical installations.

◆ GROUNDING / EARTHING
✓ Grounding → Provides a low-resistance path for unwanted electric current to Earth, helping protect people and equipment.

◆ FUSE
✓ Fuse → Safety device containing a wire designed to melt when excessive current flows, breaking the circuit.

✓ KEY IDEA → Electrical safety depends on insulation, correct circuit protection, grounding and responsible use.
